meta.subtitle: Q2 FY26 10-Q: revenue +10% to $11.99B, adjusted EPS +13%, margins expanding; the stock sits near its 52-week high at 35.4x trailing earnings

analystCommentary: We rate Thermo Fisher HOLD with a 12-month target range of $610 to $740, bracketing our $670 base case against a current price of $658.92. The second quarter was strong: revenue grew 10% to $11.99 billion, GAAP diluted EPS rose 9% to $4.68, and adjusted EPS rose 13% to $6.03, with GAAP operating margin up 0.5 point to 17.4%. Organic growth was 5% in the quarter, with acquisitions adding 5 points and currency 1 point, so half the reported top-line gain came from the Clario and filtration-and-separation deals rather than underlying volume. Management cites strengthening customer activity across pharma and biotech, academic and government, industrial and applied, and diagnostics and healthcare. The problem for new money is price, not performance: the shares trade at 35.4x trailing earnings and near the top of their $435.27 to $671.47 52-week range, and the Street's consensus target of $649.96 sits 1.4% below the current price even as 24 of 29 analysts rate the stock Buy. Our base case assumes mid-single-digit organic growth and continued PPI-driven margin gains earn a price close to consensus; our bull case ($760) requires organic acceleration and a re-rating; our bear case ($545, about 17% below spot) reflects end-market softness, government-funding disruption, or multiple compression. Probability-weighted upside is roughly flat, and reward-to-risk is unattractive at today's price. We would build positions on weakness rather than chase the high.

executiveSummary.companyOverview: Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc., founded in 1956 and headquartered in Waltham, Massachusetts, is a diversified provider of life-sciences tools, analytical instruments, specialty diagnostics, and laboratory products and biopharma services. The company operates through four segments: Life Sciences Solutions, Analytical Instruments, Specialty Diagnostics, and Laboratory Products and Biopharma Services. Its brands include Thermo Scientific, Applied Biosystems, Invitrogen, Gibco, Fisher Scientific, Unity Lab Services, Patheon and PPD. Life Sciences Solutions supplies reagents, instruments and consumables for biological and medical research and for the discovery and production of drugs and vaccines. Analytical Instruments provides instruments, consumables, software and services to pharmaceutical, biotechnology, academic, government, environmental and industrial customers as well as clinical laboratories. Specialty Diagnostics offers clinical diagnostic products, immunodiagnostics, microbiology and transplant-diagnostics testing, and a healthcare market channel. Laboratory Products and Biopharma Services covers laboratory products, the research and safety market channel, and pharma services and clinical research. Laboratory Products and Biopharma Services and Life Sciences Solutions are the two higher-revenue segments, with Analytical Instruments and Specialty Diagnostics smaller; the second-quarter revenue and margin detail by segment is set out in the financials section. The company reported FY25 revenue of $44.6 billion and serves pharmaceutical and biotech, academic and government, industrial and applied, and healthcare and diagnostics end markets.

thesis.body: Thermo Fisher is a high-quality compounder whose operating performance is not in question; the question is whether the current price leaves room for return. Second-quarter revenue grew 10% to $11.99 billion and adjusted EPS grew 13% to $6.03, with GAAP operating margin up 0.5 point to 17.4% on productivity gains from the PPI Business System. Consensus still points to mid-single-digit revenue growth and further earnings gains across FY26 and FY27, quantified in the growth section. The stock, however, trades at 35.4x trailing earnings and near the high end of its 52-week range, and the Street's own consensus target sits below the current $658.92. On next-twelve-month earnings the shares already discount continued mid-single-digit organic growth and steady margin expansion; delivery would roughly earn the current price rather than beat it. We see a balanced setup of genuine execution against a full valuation, and rate the shares HOLD, preferring to add on pullbacks.

catalysts: Updated 2026 guidance: management deferred its 2026 outlook to the earnings call, and a raise on the strength of first-half results would validate the consensus revenue and EPS estimates for the year.
Organic acceleration: quarterly organic growth of 5% is the swing factor; a step-up in pharma-and-biotech and instrument demand would lift the segments beyond the acquisition-led reported growth.

Portfolio reshaping: the March 2026 Clario acquisition and the announced divestiture of the microbiology business can reset the growth and margin mix of Laboratory Products and Biopharma Services and Specialty Diagnostics.
Capital return: the company repurchased $1.0 billion of stock in the quarter, and continued buybacks against roughly $6.3 billion of FY25 free cash flow would support per-share earnings.
Margin trajectory: adjusted operating margin reached 22.8% in the quarter, up 0.9 point year over year, and further PPI-driven productivity would compound earnings growth ahead of revenue.
risks: Valuation: the shares trade near their recent highs at a full trailing and forward multiple, leaving little margin for disappointment if growth slows.
Government funding: the October 2025 federal shutdown highlights the exposure of academic, government and healthcare customers to budget delays that can defer instrument orders.
Acquisition dependence: half of the quarter's reported revenue growth came from M&A, so slower dealmaking or weaker organic demand would materially reduce top-line growth.
China and currency: international operations expose revenue to tariffs, Chinese local-supplier rules and exchange-rate swings that can move reported results in either direction.
Leverage: the acquisition strategy is funded partly with debt, leaving limited room for further debt-funded deals without pressuring interest coverage.

financials.incomeCommentary: Second-quarter revenue was $11,994 million, up 10% from $10,855 million a year earlier; for the six months ended June 27, 2026 revenue was $22,999 million, up 8% from $21,219 million. Organic revenue growth was {+5%+} in the quarter and {+3%+} for the half, with acquisitions adding 5 points and 4 points and currency 1 point and 2 points respectively, so acquisitions accounted for half of the reported quarterly growth. GAAP operating income rose {+14% to $2,087 million+} in the quarter, lifting GAAP operating margin {+0.5 point to 17.4%+} from 16.9%; adjusted operating income rose {+15% to $2,735 million+} at a 22.8% margin. Management attributes the margin gain to strong productivity improvements from the PPI Business System, offset in part by unfavorable business mix. GAAP diluted EPS was $4.68, up 9%, and adjusted EPS was $6.03, up 13%; the gap between the two is driven mainly by $485 million of acquisition-related intangible amortization in the quarter. By segment in the quarter, Life Sciences Solutions revenue rose to $2,815 million at a 37.0% income margin; Analytical Instruments rose 7% to $1,847 million with income margin up {+4.2 points to 23.0%+}; Specialty Diagnostics rose 6% to $1,205 million at 27.7%; and Laboratory Products and Biopharma Services rose 12% to $6,693 million at 14.0%, aided by the March 2026 Clario acquisition; intersegment eliminations were $565 million. This compares with FY25 revenue of $44.6 billion and diluted EPS of $17.74. Note that the vendor's free-source data treats the company as a single consolidated segment for FY25; the segment figures here are taken from the 10-Q and press release.
financials.balanceCommentary: The balance sheet carries meaningful leverage that funds the company's acquisition strategy. At FY25, total debt was $42.7 billion and net debt $32.9 billion, up from $33.3 billion and $29.3 billion at FY24 as cash and short-term investments rose to $10.1 billion from $5.6 billion. Total equity grew to $53.4 billion from $49.6 billion, and the current ratio improved to 1.89 at FY25 from 1.66 a year earlier; on a trailing-twelve-month basis the current ratio is 1.55. Interest coverage was 5.6x on a trailing basis. The 10-Q shows six-month interest expense of $755 million and interest income of $440 million, so net interest is a real drag on pre-tax income; quarterly interest expense of $401 million was little changed from $404 million a year earlier, while quarterly interest income fell to $207 million from $297 million a year earlier. The step-up in debt through FY25 coincides with a heavier acquisition cadence, including the September 2025 filtration-and-separation purchase and the March 2026 Clario acquisition. Leverage is manageable given consistent cash generation, but it leaves less room for large debt-funded deals without pressuring coverage.
financials.cashflowCommentary: Cash generation is strong but was lighter in FY25. Operating cash flow was $7.8 billion in FY25, down from $8.7 billion in FY24, and free cash flow was $6.3 billion versus $7.3 billion, taking the FCF margin down to 14.1% from 16.9%. Capital expenditure has stepped down over the series, from $2.5 billion in FY21 to about $1.5 billion in FY25. The interim results show cash flow running higher: second-quarter operating cash flow was $2,125 million versus $1,399 million a year earlier, and quarterly free cash flow was $1,678 million against $1,105 million, after $450 million of property, plant and equipment purchases. On capital return, the company paid $0.6 billion of dividends and repurchased $3.0 billion of stock in FY25, and it repurchased $1.0 billion of stock in the second quarter of 2026. The dividend yield is only 0.29%, so buybacks, not dividends, are the primary channel for returning cash. Free cash flow comfortably covers the dividend and leaves room for opportunistic repurchases alongside debt-funded M&A.

valuation.multiplesCommentary: Thermo Fisher trades at 35.4x trailing earnings and 5.3x sales, with no EV/EBITDA figure available in the pack. On forward estimates the multiple compresses to 26.2x next-twelve-month earnings and about 23.9x FY27 consensus EPS of $27.54, reflecting expected earnings growth from $17.74 in FY25 toward $25.13 in FY26 and $27.54 in FY27. The absolute multiple is full: the stock sits near its 52-week high of $671.47, and even after forward compression the shares are not cheap for a company growing revenue in the mid-single digits organically. The Street is constructive in rating but not in price. 24 of 29 analysts rate the stock Buy, yet the consensus target of $649.96 (median $650.00) sits 1.4% below the current $658.92, within a wide range of $520.00 to $780.00. Peer multiples are not available in this pack, so the comparison is against the company's own forward earnings power rather than a peer set. Our target range of $610 to $740 brackets a base case near consensus; paying up here requires confidence that organic growth accelerates or that margins expand faster than the PPI cadence has recently delivered.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: Organic growth accelerates above the recent 5% quarterly pace as pharma-and-biotech and instrument demand strengthen, adjusted operating margin extends beyond 22.8% on PPI productivity, and the market pays a premium multiple on FY27 EPS of $27.54, pushing the shares toward the top of the Street's $520.00 to $780.00 range.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Mid-single-digit organic growth continues alongside acquisition contribution, EPS reaches roughly the consensus estimates for FY26 and FY27, and the multiple holds near 26x forward earnings, leaving the shares close to the consensus target of $649.96 and our $670 base value.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: End-market demand softens, whether a government-funding impasse like the October 2025 shutdown, weaker China and industrial spending, or slower pharma capex; organic growth stalls, and the multiple compresses from 35.4x trailing, taking the shares about 17% below the current $658.92 toward the lower end of the Street's range.

valuation.scenarioCommentary: We weight the base case at 45%, the bull at 30% and the bear at 25%. The probability-weighted fair value lands close to the current price, so expected upside is roughly flat, while the bear case at $545 implies about 17% downside, a reward-to-risk that does not favor new money at today's level. The base case is not demanding: it assumes the mid-single-digit organic growth and PPI-driven margin gains already on display continue, and that the multiple holds near 26x forward earnings, leaving the stock near the Street's consensus target. The bull case requires the two levers that would justify the current multiple, organic acceleration and faster margin expansion, to work together; that is plausible given strengthening end markets but is not yet in the reported numbers, where acquisitions still supply half of growth. The bear case is a genuine scenario rather than a formality: academic, government and healthcare customers are exposed to budget cycles, the October 2025 federal shutdown is a live reminder, and a de-rating from today's trailing multiple would hurt even without an earnings miss. The balance of these outcomes supports a HOLD and the target range set above.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: The vendor's free-source data reports Thermo Fisher as a single consolidated segment, but the 10-Q discloses four operating segments, and this report uses the filing's segment detail, set out with revenue and margins in the financials section. Life Sciences Solutions runs a high income margin on its consumables-and-bioproduction mix, well above the thinner margin in the higher-revenue Laboratory Products and Biopharma Services; Analytical Instruments and Specialty Diagnostics fall between the two, and both widened their income margins in the quarter. The mix spans consumables, instruments, diagnostics and services, giving the consolidated business diversification across end markets and a large recurring-revenue base under brands including Thermo Scientific, Invitrogen, Gibco, Fisher Scientific, PPD and Patheon.

moatFactors.name: Scale and portfolio breadth
moatFactors.body: With FY25 revenue of $44.6 billion across four segments and brands from Thermo Scientific and Applied Biosystems to Fisher Scientific, PPD and Patheon, the company offers a breadth of products and services few competitors match. Scale supports research and development, global manufacturing and a low-cost sourcing base under the PPI Business System.

moatFactors.name: Switching costs and recurring consumables
moatFactors.body: A large share of revenue is consumables, reagents and services that recur with customers' research and production workflows. Once instruments and workflows are installed, customers face validation and switching costs that make demand sticky, evident in the consumable-heavy Life Sciences Solutions segment and its strong segment income margin.

moatFactors.name: Commercial engine and distribution
moatFactors.body: The Fisher Scientific channel and the company's commercial reach give it a distribution advantage across pharma, academic, industrial and healthcare customers. Management describes an unparalleled commercial engine and cites continued share gain as end markets strengthen.

moatFactors.name: Productivity system (PPI)
moatFactors.body: The PPI Business System drives price realization, cost efficiency and margin expansion, and both GAAP and adjusted operating margins widened again in the quarter on productivity. This is a repeatable operating advantage, but one that competitors' lean programs can partly replicate.

businessMoat.durability: The moat is durable because it rests on structural features rather than a single product cycle. Revenue is diversified across four segments and multiple end markets, pharma and biotech, academic and government, industrial and applied, and diagnostics and healthcare, so weakness in one channel is often offset elsewhere; in the six months ended June 27, 2026, academic-and-government and diagnostics revenue were flat while pharma-and-biotech and industrial grew. The consumables and services base recurs, and the Fisher Scientific distribution channel is hard to replicate at scale. The main threats to durability are cyclicality in instrument demand tied to customer capital budgets and government funding, and the company's reliance on acquisitions for a meaningful share of growth, which introduces integration and valuation risk. Currency and China exposure add variability but not a structural threat. On balance we assign a WIDE moat, with the caveat that the productivity-driven margin gains supporting the premium multiple must continue for the rating to hold.

points: Reported revenue grew 10% to $11,994 million in the second quarter and 8% to $22,999 million over the six-month period, a healthy top line even as organic growth ran at 5% and 3% respectively.
Consensus expects revenue to rise from $44.6 billion in FY25 to about $47.9 billion in FY26 (+7%) and $50.3 billion in FY27, with EPS climbing from $17.74 to $25.13 and $27.54.

Acquisitions are a core growth engine: Clario (March 2026) added $441 million of clinical-research revenue in the quarter, which the filing attributes primarily to the deal, while bioproduction grew $196 million on stronger pharma-and-biotech demand alongside the September 2025 filtration-and-separation acquisition.

Margin expansion adds to earnings growth beyond revenue: continued PPI-driven productivity lifted both GAAP and adjusted operating margins in the quarter, so adjusted EPS grew faster than reported revenue.

New products support the instrument franchise, including the next-generation Orbitrap Tribrid Apex and Orbitrap Excedion mass spectrometers and the Applied Biosystems PowerFlex Thermal Cycler introduced in the quarter.

management.leadership: Marc N. Casper is chairman and chief executive officer; effective March 1, 2026 he became Chairman and CEO, and Gianluca Pettiti was promoted to President and Chief Operating Officer. The finance leadership changed in the same window: Stephen Williamson retired as Senior Vice President and Chief Financial Officer effective March 31, 2026, and James R. Meyer succeeded him as SVP and CFO as of March 1, 2026. Two other senior executives, Michel Lagarde (Executive Vice President and Chief Operating Officer) and Frederick Lowery (Executive Vice President), left the company in early 2026. The concentration of leadership transitions, a new CFO, a new president/COO and two senior departures within months, is worth monitoring, though Casper's continuity at the top and the internal promotion of Pettiti temper the risk. Management frames the strategy around three pillars: high-impact innovation, trusted-partner status with customers, and its commercial engine, supported by the PPI Business System for productivity.
management.capitalAllocation: Capital allocation tilts toward acquisitions and buybacks over dividends. In FY25 the company generated $6.3 billion of free cash flow, paid $0.6 billion in dividends and repurchased $3.0 billion of stock; the dividend yield is just 0.29%. In the second quarter of 2026 it repurchased $1.0 billion of stock. M&A is central: the September 2025 acquisition of the filtration-and-separation business from Solventum strengthened bioproduction, and the March 2026 Clario acquisition added clinical-research capabilities, while the company has announced the divestiture of its microbiology business to prune the portfolio. This acquisitive posture is funded partly with debt, so the balance between deals, buybacks and the leverage set out in the balance-sheet review is the key capital-allocation discipline to watch; interest coverage leaves headroom but not unlimited room for further debt-funded transactions.
management.governance: Governance is grounded in the company's 2026 proxy statement (DEF 14A). The Corporate Governance Guidelines require that a majority of directors and each member of the Audit, Compensation and Nominating & Corporate Governance committees be independent, applying NYSE and SEC standards plus the company's categorical criteria. After review, the Board determined that 10 directors qualify as independent and that each member of those three committees is independent. The Board considers tenure in its independence review for directors with more than nine years of service. The compensation program is described as performance-based, shareholder-aligned and market-competitive, with a substantial portion of executive pay at risk, and the company maintains stock ownership guidelines, a clawback policy and a CEO stock-holding requirement. These are standard, shareholder-friendly governance practices; the proxy excerpt does not disclose any related-party concerns.
management.insiderOwnership: Insider ownership is modest, as is typical for a company of this size. As of February 28, 2026, all current directors and executive officers as a group (19 individuals) beneficially owned 1,207,932 shares, less than one percent of shares outstanding; CEO Marc N. Casper held 449,661 shares including options and restricted stock units. The major disclosed holders are index managers: The Vanguard Group reported 32,977,462 shares (8.87%) and BlackRock 28,329,861 shares (7.62%), though a March 2026 Schedule 13G/A notes Vanguard disaggregated its reported beneficial ownership to 0.0% following an internal reorganization. Low insider ownership means alignment rests on the compensation program's stock ownership guidelines and CEO holding requirement rather than on large personal stakes.

idiosyncratic: Acquisition dependence and integration risk: acquisitions contributed 5 of the quarter's 10 points of reported revenue growth (and 4 of the half's 8 points), so organic demand must strengthen for growth to be self-sustaining; each deal also carries integration and valuation risk, and the Clario and filtration acquisitions are still being absorbed.

Leadership transition: a new CFO (James R. Meyer, effective March 1, 2026), a newly promoted president and COO (Gianluca Pettiti), and the early-2026 departures of two senior executives concentrate management change within a short window.

Valuation and multiple compression: with the shares near their 52-week high on full trailing and forward multiples, a de-rating would weigh on the stock even if earnings meet estimates, and the Street's consensus target already sits below the current price.

Customer budget exposure: academic, government and healthcare customers depend on funding cycles, and academic-and-government and diagnostics revenue were flat in the six months ended June 27, 2026, showing demand can stall even while other markets grow.

Leverage: the debt that funds the acquisition strategy, quantified in the balance-sheet review, leaves limited room for further debt-funded M&A without pressuring interest coverage, and a downturn in cash generation would tighten that further.
risks.systemic: Systemic risks are largely macro and geopolitical. The company flags that its served markets can experience cyclical downturns and that general economic conditions and elevated inflation affect demand, order cancellations and pricing. International operations expose it to currency swings, with currency translation adding $0.37 billion to 2025 revenue and able to reverse, as well as tariffs, trade measures and Chinese regulations favoring local suppliers. Government funding is a specific channel of macro risk: the October 2025 federal shutdown illustrates how budget impasses can delay or reduce spending by academic, government and healthcare customers. Public health emergencies are a two-sided risk, having driven both demand and disruption in the past. None of these is unique to Thermo Fisher, but its scale and international footprint mean broad economic or trade shocks would show up in reported results.

body: We rate Thermo Fisher HOLD with a 12-month target range of $610 to $740 around a $670 base case, against the current price of $658.92. The business is performing: second-quarter revenue grew 10% to $11.99 billion, adjusted EPS grew 13% to $6.03, and margins expanded on PPI productivity, with management pointing to strengthening demand across end markets. The obstacle is price: at a full trailing and forward multiple, near its 52-week high, the shares already discount continued execution, and the Street's consensus target sits below the current price even with a majority of analysts rating the stock Buy.

Our probability-weighted fair value is close to today's price, so expected upside is roughly flat while the bear case at $545 implies about 17% downside, an unattractive reward-to-risk for new capital. We would accumulate on pullbacks toward the lower half of our target range, where the quality of the franchise, the recurring consumables base and the WIDE moat justify a long-term position, rather than pay up near the high. Key things to watch are organic growth stepping above the recent 5% pace, the pace of PPI-driven margin expansion, and the balance between debt-funded M&A and buybacks against the company's net-debt load.
